lesson_1.title: Introduction to Recursion: Factorial
task: Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem. Every recursive function requires a 'base case' to terminate the execution and prevent infinite loops.
1. Define the base case: if the integer is 0 or 1, terminate recursion and return 1.
2. Define the recursive step: multiply the current integer by a subsequent function call evaluated at the integer minus one.
3. Otherwise, return the product of `n` and `factorial(n - 1)`.

2. Create a list containing only the current integer.

task: Binary Search is a highly efficient algorithm for finding an item in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search space in half, resulting in an O(log n) time complexity.

lesson_3.title: Divide Methodology: Array Halving

lesson_3.title: Conquer Methodology: Merge Protocol
task: The 'Conquer' phase of Merge Sort relies on a helper function that evaluates two already-sorted arrays and merges them into a single, contiguous sorted array using pointer logic.
1. Initialize a new list to act as the combined payload.
2. Deploy dual pointers to evaluate the current elements of both lists simultaneously.
3. Append the lesser element to the new list and advance its respective pointer.
4. When one list is exhausted, append the remaining elements of the other list.
3. Loop while `i < len(left)` and `j < len(right)`. If `left[i] < right[j]`, append `left[i]` and increment `i`. Otherwise, append `right[j]` and increment `j`.
4. Extend the `result` list with any remaining elements: `left[i:]` and `right[j:]`.

optimizations.title: Optimization: Linear to Logarithmic Search
task: A linear scan (O(n)) through a sorted array is highly inefficient for large datasets, as it checks elements sequentially. Refactoring the traversal into a Binary Search structure reduces the time complexity to a rapid O(log n).
1. Analyze the current implementation: the `for` loop evaluates every item, creating an O(n) performance bottleneck.
3. Introduce `low` and `high` pointer variables to establish boundaries.
4. Implement a `while` loop that calculates the exact middle (`mid = (low + high) // 2`). Check the midpoint, and adjust the boundaries to systematically halve the search space.
5. Observe the analytical metrics demonstrating the transition to O(log n) efficiency.

optimizations.title: Optimization: Finding Peak Element
task: A peak element is an integer strictly greater than its adjacent neighbors. Instead of an O(n) sequential scan, we can deploy a modified binary search to intuitively follow the increasing mathematical slope in O(log n) time.
1. Eliminate the inefficient O(n) sequential loop.
3. Within a `while low < high` loop, compute the midpoint index.
4. Evaluate the slope: if `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, the slope is increasing to the right. Adjust the `low` pointer up (`mid + 1`).
5. If the slope is decreasing, the peak exists in the left partition. Reduce the `high` pointer to `mid`.
6. Return the `low` pointer index when the iteration concludes.

optimizations.title: Optimization: Iteration Over Recursion
task: Recursive implementations of Binary Search consume memory via the call stack by saving state for every nested function call, resulting in an O(log n) space complexity. Converting the recursion into an iterative loop optimizes this to O(1).
1. Identify the memory stack generated by returning the function within itself (e.g., `return search_optimized(...)`).
2. Remove all recursive function calls from the structure.
3. Refactor the core logic using an iterative `while low <= high:` loop structure.
4. Reassign the `low` and `high` pointer variables directly within the active loop instead of passing them as parameters to a new function.
5. Verify through the analyzer that the Space Complexity has successfully dropped to O(1).
